passage: Everyone in Class 9 knew me: I'm the boy who lends pens and carries the cricket kit. When the captain election was announced, I told myself the votes were already mine. I made no poster and wrote no speech, and on nomination day I skipped the class visits to play cricket. Gurleen, my rival, went from room to room with a two-line promise about a working water cooler and a library corner, and she even visited the Class 6 and 7 rows, which I had never thought of. On result day my friends were shocked. I lost by forty votes. I sat on the steps thinking: they liked me, but nobody knew what I would do. I'm Sandeep, and I have not forgotten that feeling.

qa.q: By how many votes did Sandeep lose?
What was Sandeep feeling on the steps, and what did the loss show?
qa.a: Sandeep felt shocked and let down, and saw that being liked was not enough because nobody knew what Sandeep would do.

qa.q: What could Sandeep have done differently, and why?
qa.a: Sandeep could have visited every class with one clear proposal and asked what students needed, because votes follow a plan people can picture.

qa.q: How might a Class 7 student have seen the two candidates?
qa.a: A Class 7 student would have seen Gurleen visit and speak clearly, while Sandeep never came, so Gurleen would seem the more serious choice.

grounding: A well-liked student assumes friends will vote for them and makes no plan, and rivals with clear proposals reach more classes, so the student loses despite a lot of goodwill.
